master_predictions.verdict: The son is at his mother's own house, not at his master's; she will find him there on her coming home, and will see him on the very day the two significators perfect their trine (25 July, about 2–3 p.m.). On the companion queries from the same figure: the absent party is alive and in health, with news in about ten weeks (ten days if near).
reasoning_points: Jupiter, lord of the 5th (the son), is in the Ascendant/east angle — the party sought is at the mother's home
Moon applies to a sextile of Saturn, lord of the 4th (the querent's dwelling)
Had Jupiter been in the 10th (the master's house), judgment would have been the reverse (Lilly states the counterfactual rule)
Jupiter (son's significator, per the further explanation) and Venus (mother's) perfecting a trine by ephemeris times the meeting/news
For the absent-alive query: Moon and Venus free from evil aspect of the lord of the 8th, a benefic in the Ascendant, Venus in the 9th — pronounce the absent in health
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'I judged that she would find him there at her coming home: which she did'; and of the trine day, 'therefore I judged that she should see him at that time: which she did.' The 1647 further explanation adds she reached home about 3 p.m. that day and found her son abiding her coming.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, the example figure resolving four queries (1st: if a party might be found at home; 4th: if one absent be dead or alive) — 1647 pp.190ff in modern reprint pagination; Fig. 3 in the 1852 Zadkiel edition

master_predictions.verdict: He shall acquire a competent estate and live in good rank among his neighbours, but by labour and care; he is advised to marry, for without marriage he shall not so well subsist; the wealth will come partly by his own industry and partly by a wife's fortune, beginning in about two years, with very great trading about 1640; and it will continue — he shall never be reduced to want.
reasoning_points: Most planets, especially the fortunes, swift, well posited and unafflicted; Venus lady of the Ascendant near Regulus; Moon increasing in light; Jupiter almost culminating — general testimony of good rank

Mars, lord of the 2nd and of the Part of Fortune, in the Ascendant near Spica (18° Libra); Jupiter in exaltation angular, his square to the Ascendant counting as a trine in signs of long ascension; Moon transferring the light of Mars and Mercury to Venus, the querent's significator — he will acquire an estate, but an infortune (Mars) as significator means by labour
Mars is also lord of the 7th (marriage) and the chief significator of the wealth demanded — hence: marry
Means: Mars in the Ascendant = his own industry; Mars lord of the 7th = a wife's good fortune; Moon lady of the 10th (trade) transferring light = diligence in his profession

Time: significators oriental and five planets swift = soon; Mars about 2° from the Ascendant = about two years to a portion with his wife; Moon wanting 6°27' of her conjunction with Venus = about 1640 for very great trading
Continuance: cusp of the 2nd a fixed sign, Part of Fortune therein, Jupiter exalted and angular, Venus and Moon in the fixed sign Leo
Caution added: Sun, lord of the 11th, square the Part of Fortune and the cusp of the 2nd — avoid confiding in 'solar men' (friends)
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'And so to this day he hath [attained it by labour]'; 'He has since had a good fortune with his wife, money, and land, and been very successful in trade'; the two-year timing matched his wife's portion.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, chapter on 2nd-house questions (whether the querent shall be rich), example figure of the London tradesman

master_predictions.verdict: Yes — Lilly judged he should buy the houses, proceed in the matter and in the end conclude for them, though slowly and with many meetings and trouble; the seller would not abate one penny of the £530 demanded; money would be procured by borrowing (a friend would lend £500 shortly after Mercury turned direct), not from his own funds.
reasoning_points: The ascending degree was the same degree as a planet in Lilly's own radix — taken as a good omen
Sun, the seller's significator, in the 7th received in exaltation and no other purchaser about it — the seller is high in his demands and in no necessity to sell, but no rival buyer
Lord of the 7th is also lord of the 11th (hopes) — hopes not frustrated
Venus applying to a trine of Saturn, lord of the 4th (the houses), with no abscission or frustration before perfection — a main strong argument he should buy
Moon translating light by a square out of signs of long ascension — he will go on and probably contract, but slowly and with trouble
Mars, lord of his 2nd, retrograde — he will get none of his own money for the purchase (confirmed: he did not)
Mercury entering his exaltation and turning direct in twelve days — hopes of procuring money then
Quality of the houses from the 4th sign and Saturn: really old, but strong and able to stand many years
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in detail in the text: the bargain was struck on 25 April following (the day Venus and the Sun came to their aspect); on 17 May he paid the £530 and his conveyance was sealed — 'six weeks and some days from the time of the Question'; a friend lent him £500 twelve days after (when Mercury turned direct). Lilly adds he did himself injury in money by the bargain but never repented it.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

master_predictions.verdict: The report is false: 'All that we heard was untruth, and the Town neither was, or should be taken by Him or his Forces'; the news were lies, devolving to division among the enemy and no benefit to them.
reasoning_points: The angles are all moveable, and Saturn vitiates the cusp of the 10th and Mars the cusp of the 7th — one argument the report is false
Moon cadent, in a sign wherein she nothing delights — a second strong evidence of a false rumour
Sun on the cusp of the Ascendant — a sign of good to the Parliament, the 1st house signifying that party
Lady of the Ascendant, significatrix of the querent's side, in her exaltation; lord of the 7th (the enemy) entering his fall and afflicted — the enemy weakened
Moon separating from the lord of the 7th and transferring light to a benefic — good to come to 'us' from the report, and division/treason among the enemy
master_predictions.outcome: Not stated as a postscript in the excerpt, but a matter of historical record: Cambridge was never taken by the King during the Civil War (it remained a Parliamentarian stronghold, headquarters of the Eastern Association). Marked as externally verified, not Lilly-stated.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. XXXI 'If a Report or common Rumour were True or False' (1647 pp.204–208)

master_predictions.verdict: The ship is not lost but living; she has lately been in danger (a leak or damage near her breast) but is now recovered and in harbour to repair, south-west from London on our own coasts or near those between Ireland and Wales; the sailors and officers are safe; news or certain discovery of her will come that night or within two days; and the merchant shall gain by the adventure.
reasoning_points: Saturn's square from a cardinal sign out of the 11th, very near the Ascendant, and Saturnine fixed stars afflict the ship's body — the ship is of Saturn's nature, sluggish, heavy, not very sound; Cancer a weakly sign agrees
Cauda (South Node) in the 9th and Saturn in Aries (the ship's breast) — she has been in distress on the voyage, by a leak or damage near her breast

Moon, lady of the Ascendant, in the 11th in her exaltation, unimpedited, applying by benevolent trine to Sun and Mercury and near the body of Jupiter; all significators above the earth and no infortunes in angles — ship, sailors and officers safe and in good condition

Place: Moon fixed and in the 11th; Taurus a southern sign in an east quarter verging south; Mercury in Capricorn, a south sign and west angle — south-west from London, on our own coasts between Ireland and Wales; a fixed sign and the 11th (house of comfort) — she is in some harbour, put in to repair
Time: Moon, Sun and Mercury all swift and wanting but a few minutes of a perfect trine — news that night or within two days
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: '(It proved that she was in a harbour in the west)' and of the news, '(And so it proved.)'

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

master_predictions.verdict: Loss to the merchant: he will lose much, if not all, in this ship; she is cast away (sunk).
reasoning_points: Moon lately separated from a square of Saturn, lord of the 8th and 9th — the ship had lately been in danger of shipwreck
Moon then void of course (hence no news heard of her), in a cadent house, applying to no benefic
Moon afterwards applying to a trine of Saturn — still lord of the 8th — and then to opposition of Mercury, lord of the 12th and 4th, Mercury in his detriment and entering combustion
Jupiter, dispositor of Mercury, subterranean and conjunct Mars in the term of an infortune; Mars in his fall near the cusp of the 2nd — loss to the merchant
Part of Fortune in the 6th, disposed of by retrograde afflicted Jupiter in the 2nd, Jupiter in no aspect to it, Moon and Mercury also in square to it
The principal significator in the 4th and afflicted — a sure sign of the ship sinking
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'I judged he would lose much, if not all, in this ship; and so consequently that she was cast away. (And so it proved.)'

master_predictions.verdict: Victory will be ours (Waller's Parliamentarian side); the enemy will be worsted, with loss and dishonour to Hopton; we shall take a considerable proportion of their ammunition though not a perfect victory without some diminution; perfect and satisfactory news will arrive within eleven or twelve hours of the question.
reasoning_points: Moon, having principal signification of us and our army, in her exaltation with Jupiter — all is and will be well on our side
Moon separating from Jupiter — we have already taken some ammunition from them or performed some service against them
Sun, lord of our substance and assistants, in the 10th in the very degree of his exaltation (19° Aries) — success and assistance
Proximity of Saturn to the Sun — we shall not gain the whole; a considerable proportion only

Moon applying to Venus and then to a sextile of Mercury (angular), swift and increasing in light, 11° distant from Venus — news within eleven or twelve hours (hours, not days, because the fight was within fifty miles of London)

Saturn, Hopton's significator, sub radiis, in his fall, in no aspect to any planet, wholly peregrine and unfortunate, aspecting the cusp of the 7th by square — loss to his army and dishonour to himself; only Mars and Cauda in the 9th — Hopton had no supplies ready
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'It appeared, by a letter from the army on that same Friday, that our generals took on the previous day 120 commanders and gentlemen, 560 common soldiers, and much ammunition.' (Historically: the Battle of Cheriton, 29 March 1644, was a Parliamentarian victory.)

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II (Fig. 20 in the 1852 edition): 'A Figure erected to know whether Sir William Waller or Sir Ralph Hopton should overcome'

master_predictions.verdict: Essex shall obtain and take Reading, and gain glory and honour thereby — but with much difficulty and some fighting, and rather by composition (negotiated surrender) than by blood; the King will oppose and send relief forces with all vigour but shall not prevail; the town is strong and wants no ammunition; the way to force surrender is to set division among the principal officers against their chief; about eight days from the question they would begin to treat, and Essex would be master of the town.
reasoning_points: Mars, Essex's significator, excellently fortified, labouring under no misfortune except being in his fall; in warfare it is of great consequence to have Mars friendly to the querent
Moon void of course — little hope of gaining it in that time; Moon applying to a sextile of Mars (equivalent to a square in signs of long ascension) — much difficulty and some fighting first
Mars and Moon in mutual reception (Mars in her house, Moon in his terms and face, near Regulus, in the 10th) — he shall take Reading and gain honour
Sun, the King's significator, in the 7th in a fixed sign — the King will oppose and send relief, but Mars is better fortified than the Sun, so he shall not prevail
Aquarius (town) not afflicted — the town strong and able to hold out; Venus in the 5th — they want not ammunition

Saturn, lord of the 4th (the Governor), in his fall and beheld by Mars — sowing division among the officers is the assured way to occasion the surrender; timing from the significators' separation from their sextile and the Moon's direct application, in cardinal signs — about eight days to treating, surrender by composition because the aspects were separating rather than violent
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'The Town was delivered for the Parliament's use the 27th of April... three days after the time limited by me was expired; but the very Monday before, being eight days after the Figure set, they began to treat.' Lilly adds the King's relief was beaten back at Caversham Bridge, the Governor (Aston) was hurt in the head (as Saturn in Pisces(?) afflicted by Mars denoted), and they did not want ammunition, as Venus in the 5th signified. See the year flag in inputs (1643 historically; OCR prints 1644).

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXVI 'If his Excellency Robert Earl of Essex should take Reading' (1647 pp.401–405)

master_predictions.verdict: Search west: the dog is westward from the owner's house at Temple Bar — about Long Acre or the upper part of Drury Lane, within the lines of communication (not gone out of the parish/quarter); he is indoors, in some chamber or upper room, kept privately and in great secrecy; the owner shall have his dog again, or news of him, on the Monday following or near that time.
reasoning_points: The sign of the 6th is west-and-by-south and the quarter of heaven is west; the dog's significator is in a western sign but southern quarter tending west; the Moon is in a south-west sign verging to the western angle — the plurality of testimonies signifies west

The dog's significator in a sign of the same triplicity as the Ascendant (which signifies London) and applying to a trine of the cusp of the 6th — the dog is not out of the lines of communication but in the same quarter
The significator's sign being an airy sign — the dog is in some chamber or upper room; the Moon under the Sun's beams and Sun and Moon in the 8th — kept privately, in great secrecy
The Sun on Monday following applying by dexter aspect to Saturn, lord of the Ascendant, and the Moon to the dog's significator, having exaltation in the Ascendant — recovery or news on that Monday
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: a gentleman of the querent's acquaintance, coming by accident to see a friend in Long Acre, found the dog tied up under a table, knew it to be the querent's, and sent it home that same Monday about ten in the morning — 'to my very great credit.'

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXII 'A Dog missing, Where?' (1647 pp.400/594 in reprint pagination)

master_predictions.verdict: The servant went westward at his first departing and is now west from his master's house — full west or a little to the south, near a great water (the Thames), at Kingston upon Thames; he shall be recovered within a day or two, and the master shall not lose his goods/servant.
reasoning_points: At the time of flight the Moon was in a western sign, and the servant's significator is still in the same sign; Mercury, the common significator of servants, in a western sign (south quarter) — he went west and is west
Mercury (servant's significator) angular and every way as strong as the Moon — judge direction by Mercury rather than the Moon
Servant's significator and lord of the Ascendant hastening to a trine out of angles — within a day or two the master shall have his servant again

Moon in the 2nd in her own house (the servant being part of the master's estate), and the Sun in the 2nd in perfect aspect with a planet in the 11th — the master shall not lose, but recover, his lost goods
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the 1852 edition's wording: 'Upon the Friday following he came home, and said he had been at Kingston upon Thames; which if true, then he was full West, or a little to the South, and near a great Water, viz. the Thames.'

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXI 'Of Fugitive Servant, which way gone, when return'

master_predictions.verdict: Yes — the match can and shall be brought on again and effected, to the content of both parties, within twenty days, if it is worked through a particular intermediary: a Saturn-described gentleman of quality (an intimate acquaintance of the suitor) must be fully acquainted with her folly and interpose; all things must be hastened before the Saturn–Mars aspect is over (27 June), and the gentleman suitor should first move in the business on 19 June near noon, when Jupiter and Saturn are in perfect sextile.
reasoning_points: The lady's own state read from the figure first: Saturn, lord of the 7th, in the south angle conjunct Mars in a fixed earthy sign, elevated — the gentleman is sad, angry, much discontented, scorning his former slights (as Saturnine people do), and incensed by a kinsman/gentleman of quality (Mars, lord of the 3rd from the 7th)

Moon separated from the gentleman's significator void of course and applying to opposition of the Sun, with no reception between the significators — small hopes by her own direct means; she had undone herself by her own perverseness
Yet reception between Venus and the Moon and between the Sun and Venus; the Moon disposing of Saturn in her exaltation; Saturn near a dexter sextile of Jupiter, still applying

Main occasion: Jupiter applies to a sextile of Saturn, lord of the 7th, receiving his virtue and transferring it to the Sun, lord of the Ascendant, with no prohibition, abscission or frustration until perfected (27 June) — therefore the Saturnine gentleman signified by Jupiter's mediation... i.e. the mutual acquaintance can revive the business, and timing must precede the perfected aspect
Secondary testimony: application of the two significators (lords of 1st and 7th) to a sextile, and the Moon applying to the lord of the Ascendant with reception

Lilly adds, from the same figure, that the suitor had lately been offered another match — a gentlewoman signified by Venus, of good fortune and excellent descent — and told the lady not to fear his marrying her, because Mars interposed between Venus and Saturn
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'My counsel was followed, and the issue was thus: By the Gentleman's means and procurement, the matter was brought on again, the Match effected, and all within twenty days following, to the content of the sorrowful (but as to me unthankful) Lady.'

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, 7th-house (marriage) chapters — the example judgment printed at 1647 pp.385–388, immediately before Chap. LXI

master_predictions.verdict: No — the parsonage is not to be obtained; Lilly dehorted him from proceeding further. A neighbour, by letter, words or cross information, will wholly destroy his hopes; Mercurial men (scholars or divines) will be his enemies, and some woman will inform against him or prejudice him in his suit.
reasoning_points: No aspect between Jupiter, lord of the 9th (the benefice), and the lord of the Ascendant, nor is the Moon in any aspect with him
Neither the lord of the Ascendant nor the Moon is posited in the 9th
No weighty planet translates or collects the light of Jupiter (the preferment) to the querent's significator
There is no reception between the significators
Saturn is impedited in the Ascendant and by his presence infortunes the question, causing the querent to despair of obtaining it
Moon separates from a trine and applies to an opposition of Mercury, lord of the 3rd — a neighbour with letter/words/cross information will destroy his hopes; Mercurial men his enemies
Venus in the 7th opposing the Ascendant — some woman will inform against him or prejudice his suit
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: the parson 'being covetous would proceed further... and when he thought to have the matter absolutely on his side, behold, a scurvy Letter, revealing some manifest truths concerning a Female, dashed the good Man's hopes' — he never discovered which neighbour had affronted him.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
source.chapter: Book II, Chap. LXXIX 'If it should obtain the Parsonage desired' (1647 pp.437–439)

master_predictions.verdict: The thief is a man whose calling is to live upon the water — a fisherman of Jupiter/Mars nature living near the Thames side, lately leaving his own house; the goods are in some low room in a moist place; there will be discovery and partial (not complete) recovery of the goods.
reasoning_points: No peregrine planet in an angle but Jupiter, on the cusp of the 7th — the peregrine planet in an angle describes the thief; Jupiter in Scorpio, a moist sign
Mercury, significator of the goods, in Pisces, a moist sign, and the Part of Fortune in Cancer, a moist sign — the thief lives by the water and the goods are in a low, moist place
Moon, lady of the Part of Fortune, applying by sextile to Mercury, lord of the 2nd — he shall hear of his goods again
But Mercury in his fall and detriment — recovery not complete; Mercury in his own terms and in trine to the Part of Fortune — hopes of regaining some of the goods

Mars, lord of the 7th, leaving Scorpio his own sign and entering another — inquire for a fisherman who had lately sold land or was leaving his own house for another; such a one was found: a mere fisherman, jovial, much suspected of thievery, answering the description
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: Lilly took out a warrant, kept it private until Sunday 18th, searched only that one house, and 'found part of my fish in water, part eaten, part not consumed; all confessed' — including seven Portugal onions the thief's wife had unknowingly made into pottage.

source.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II

master_predictions.verdict: The thief is neither of the querent's suspects: he is a youth of about 15 or 16, a neighbour's child, dwelling opposite the querent or a little south-west; the querent shall not only hear of but have his money again within four days.
reasoning_points: Mars (the querent's significator and first suspect's planet) is lord of the Ascendant in his own terms and face — a planet essentially dignified cannot signify the thief; Saturn likewise in the 7th (house of theft) in his own term and face — also passed by
Mercury, in an angle with no essential dignity, in partile conjunction with Saturn and square to Mars — Mercury signifies the thief
Sex: Moon in a masculine sign applying to a masculine planet (Mars); Mercury conjunct Saturn and square Mars, both masculine — the thief is male
Mercury ever signifies youth, and the Moon so near the Sun separating — a youth of some 15 or 16; described thin-visaged with a scar/blemish (Mars square Mercury), dark hair (closeness to Saturn)
Mercury conjunct Saturn, lord of the 3rd and 4th — the child of some neighbour; Moon and Mercury in Gemini/Taurus in the 7th — he dwelt opposite the querent or a little south-west
Part of Fortune in the Ascendant disposed of by Mars its lord in the 10th, Moon applying to Mars's sextile within about 4° — he shall have his money again within four days
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'The event proved me right, both as to the person and the return of the money, which was within three days after' — although the querent at first 'believed not one word I said.'

master_predictions.verdict: The husband's significator is wholly free from affliction — the man is unharmed; but the woman herself will die first: she will die, or be in great danger of death, about the latter end of September or the beginning of October (when Mars comes to an opposition of Saturn).
reasoning_points: The husband's significator (the Sun) is in his hayz and free from the least manner of misfortune, and so is the man from all infortune — he is alive and unharmed

For the wife: Saturn, lord of the 6th, retrograde, and her ascendant lord also lord of the 8th — she relapses from one disease into another, partly by her own obstinacy (her ascendant lord being also lord of the 8th) and partly by the physician's neglect (the physician's significator conjunct Saturn in equinoctial/tropical signs and angles arguing small care)

Timing: observing when Mars and Saturn come to an ill aspect (Mars most representing her person and conditions), Mars comes to Saturn's opposition about the latter end of September, Mars then near the Moon's place in the question — therefore she probably dies or is in great danger then
master_predictions.outcome: Confirmed in the text: 'in truth she died the eighth of October, upon which day Mars and [the other significator] were in the eighth degree...' — within days of the window Lilly had named.
